warmup.q: Your service gets 400 authorizations a second, and each one takes 250 ms from start to finish, mostly waiting on the card issuer. With one thread per request, about how many threads are busy at any moment?
options: About 400, one per request each second
warmup.why: Little's law: requests in flight = arrival rate x time in system = 400 x 0.25 s = 100. Core count only matters for work that computes. Each request is in the system for a quarter of a second, so at any moment about a quarter of one second's arrivals are inside.

sections.h: CPU-bound work wants about one thread per core
sections.html:
Here is CpuBoundDemo on a 4-core machine. The job is 32 SHA-256 tasks with no I/O and no locks, run on pools of different sizes:

availableProcessors() = 4
 1 threads:   359 ms
 2 threads:   171 ms
 4 threads:    92 ms
 8 threads:    96 ms
16 threads:    98 ms

Doubling the threads halves the time until the thread count reaches the core count. After that, nothing improves. A core runs one thread at a time, so a fifth thread on four cores only gets CPU by taking it from one of the other four. You pay for context switches and colder caches and get no extra work done.

So for CPU-bound work, size the pool to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(). Goetz suggests one more than that, so the CPUs stay busy when a thread stalls on a page fault (a pause while the operating system fetches a page of memory). Either is fine. Fifty threads for hashing is not.

Ask the JVM, not the hardware spec. On Linux the JVM's container support, on by default, reads the CPU limit from the container's cgroup (the kernel feature that enforces a pod's limits) when the JVM starts. So inside a container, availableProcessors() reports the CPU limit of the container, and a pod with a 2-CPU limit on a 64-core node sees 2. That is the number you want, because it's all the CPU the pod gets. You can override it with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N.

In a payment service, CPU-bound work is the minority: signing and verifying, encrypting card data, parsing a large settlement file, scoring a fraud model in-process. Most request handling spends its time waiting, and that needs a different rule.

try.title: Find where the curve goes flat
steps: Check how many cores your machine has. Predict the pool size after which CpuBoundDemo stops getting faster.
Run it with the command below.

code.title: CpuBoundDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l03; import java.security.MessageDigest; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { // pure computation: SHA-256 over 16 MB, like signing a big settlement file. No I/O, no locks. static long hash(long seed) throws Exception { MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"); byte[] block = new byte[16 * 1024]; block[0] = (byte) seed; for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sha.update(block); return sha.digest()[0]; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); hash(1); // warm up the JIT once for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long sum = 0; try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { List<Future<Long>> parts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int task = 0; task < 32; task++) { long seed = task; parts.add(pool.submit(() -> hash(seed))); } for (Future<Long> f : parts) sum += f.get(); } System.out.printf("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)%n", threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum); } } }

alt.title: CpuBoundDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l03 import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.concurrent.Executors // pure computation: SHA-256 over 16 MB, like signing a big settlement file. No I/O, no locks. private fun hash(seed: Long): Long { val sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") val block = ByteArray(16 * 1024) block[0] = seed.toByte() repeat(1_000) { sha.update(block) } return sha.digest()[0].toLong() } /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ fun main() { println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()) hash(1) // warm up the JIT once for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sum = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> val parts = (0 until 32).map { task -> pool.submit<Long> { hash(task.toLong()) } } parts.sumOf { it.get() } } println("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)".format(threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum)) } }

try.expect: The time roughly halves from 1 to 2 threads and from 2 to the core count, then stays flat or gets a little worse. If other programs are busy on the machine, or the laptop has slower efficiency cores, the curve flattens earlier: the pool only gets the CPU nobody else is using.

sections.h: Work that waits: N × U × (1 + W/C)
sections.html:
Most backend tasks compute briefly and then wait: for the database, the card issuer, a Kafka acknowledgement. A waiting thread uses no CPU, so while it waits, another thread can use the core. That is why pools for I/O work need more threads than cores. Goetz's formula from Java Concurrency in Practice says how many:

threads = cores x target CPU utilization x (1 + wait time / compute time)

Take 8 cores, a target of 80 percent CPU, and an authorization that computes for 20 ms (parsing, validation, signing) and then waits 180 ms for the issuer: 8 x 0.8 x (1 + 180/20) = 64 threads. The ratio is what matters. A task that waits nine times longer than it computes leaves room for about ten such tasks per core.

The formula is a starting point, and it can mislead you in three ways.

First, you have to measure W and C. A timer around the downstream call gives you W, and the rest of the task's time is roughly C. JFR shows the same split. A guess like "it's mostly I/O" gives a number that looks precise and isn't.

Second, it assumes waiting is free. Waiting on a remote call is. Waiting for a lock, or for a connection that every other thread also needs, is not: more threads just make a longer line for the same lock.

Third, it sizes for CPU and knows nothing else. It can't tell that the issuer accepts only 50 concurrent connections from you, or that your database pool has 20. Those limits often decide the answer, and the last section of this lesson is about them.

try.title: Size two pools by hand
steps: A refund service runs on 4 cores, targets 50 percent CPU, and each refund computes for 5 ms and waits 95 ms on the ledger. Work out the pool size.
A report job on the same box computes for 40 ms and waits 10 ms per row. Work out its pool size too, then check both with PoolSizing.ioBound once you've done the lab.
try.expect: Refunds: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 95/5) = 40 threads. Reports: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 10/40) = 2.5, rounded up to 3. The report job is mostly CPU, so it gets about as many threads as the cores you're willing to give it.

sections.h: Little's law: in flight = arrival rate × time in system
sections.html:
Goetz's formula starts from CPUs. Little's law starts from traffic. It holds for any stable system, a supermarket or a thread pool:

L = λ x W

L is the average number of requests inside, λ (lambda) is the arrival rate and W is the average time each request spends inside. Your payment API gets 400 authorizations a second at peak, and each takes 250 ms end to end, so 400 x 0.25 = 100 requests are in flight on average. With one thread per request, that is 100 busy threads. If you have fewer, the extra requests wait somewhere.

Turn it around to see what a pool can do. Solve for λ: 50 threads at 250 ms each finish at most 50 / 0.25 = 200 requests a second. If 400 arrive, 200 a second pile up in the queue. The waiting adds to W, so the queue grows without limit until memory or patience runs out. That is the unbounded-queue story from lesson 2 of this track, with numbers.

LittlesLawDemo checks the law with 200 requests that each wait 50 ms:

 5 threads:   97 req/s measured,  100 predicted by threads / W
10 threads:  191 req/s measured,  200 predicted by threads / W
20 threads:  376 req/s measured,  400 predicted by threads / W

When the work is waiting, throughput is threads divided by latency. Faster CPUs would not help. More threads would, for as long as threads are the scarce thing. That argument, made in JEP 444 (the JDK Enhancement Proposal for virtual threads), is why virtual threads exist, and the "Virtual threads" track picks it up.

try.title: Check Little's law
steps: Read LittlesLawDemo. Predict the throughput for 40 threads before you run it.
Run it with the command below and compare each row with its prediction.

code.title: LittlesLawDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms on a downstream call, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ public class LittlesLawDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean db = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("db"); Semaphore connections = new Semaphore(10); // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on int requests = 200; double latencySeconds = 0.050; for (int threads : new int[] {5, 10, 20, 40}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { try { if (db) connections.acquire(); try { Thread.sleep(50); // the downstream call } finally { if (db) connections.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } double seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9; System.out.printf("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W%n", threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds); } } }

alt.title: LittlesLawDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms on a downstream call, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val db = args.firstOrNull() == "db" val connections = Semaphore(10) // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on val requests = 200 val latencySeconds = 0.050 for (threads in listOf(5, 10, 20, 40)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> repeat(requests) { pool.execute { try { if (db) connections.acquire() try { Thread.sleep(50) // the downstream call } finally { if (db) connections.release() } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } } val seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 println("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W".format( threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds)) } }

try.expect: 5, 10 and 20 threads land within a few percent of 100, 200 and 400 requests a second. 40 threads falls short of 800 (about 630 here), because 200 requests are only five rounds for 40 threads and the pool's start-up time is now a large part of the run.

sections.h: The downstream decides: connection pools and bulkheads
sections.html:
Little's law counts threads, but a request in flight holds other things too. Say every authorization writes to the ledger and holds one of your 20 database connections for 10 ms. The database path then tops out at 20 / 0.01 = 2,000 writes a second, whatever your thread count. Threads beyond that line up for a connection instead of a CPU. Run the demo with db and you see it: with only 10 connections, 20 and 40 threads are no faster than 10.

So size from the scarcest resource backwards: the database pool, the issuer's contract (say 50 concurrent connections per merchant client), a fraud API's rate limit. HikariCP, a widely used JDBC connection pool, makes the same point for databases on its wiki page about pool sizing. It starts from a small formula, connections = (cores x 2) + effective spindle count, and tells you to load-test from there, because more connections than the database can serve make every query slower.

Limits also need isolation. Say authorizations, refunds and balance lookups share one pool of 64 threads, and the issuer slows from 120 ms to 3 s. Little's law fills all 64 threads with stuck issuer calls within seconds. Balance lookups, which never touch the issuer, now time out too.

A bulkhead stops that. It is a separate limit per dependency, named after the walls that keep one flooded compartment from sinking a ship. It can be a separate pool per downstream, or a Semaphore around the call, which is what you build in the lab. The issuer gets 50 permits. When they are gone, new issuer calls fail fast, and the rest of the service keeps its threads.

try.title: Hit the connection ceiling
steps: Predict the four rows of LittlesLawDemo when every request also needs one of 10 connections.
try.expect: 5 threads still give about 100 requests a second and 10 threads about 200. 20 and 40 threads also stay near 200: ten connections at 50 ms each allow 10 / 0.05 = 200 a second, and the extra threads just wait in connections.acquire().

analogy: Little's law is a supermarket. If 120 customers walk in every hour and each one spends half an hour inside, there are about 60 people in the shop at any moment. To serve more customers per hour without making anyone shop faster, you need room for more people inside, which for a pool means more threads. The checkouts are the downstream limit: add aisles all you like, and if there are four tills, people queue at the tills. The analogy breaks at the door. Shoppers who see a packed shop walk away. An unbounded queue in front of a pool never turns anyone away, so it fills up instead.
world: Write down the three numbers for your busiest path before you touch a pool setting: peak arrivals per second, average time per request, and the smallest limit it passes through. For card authorizations that is usually the issuer connection limit or the database pool, not CPU. Check what your Quarkus worker pool is set to (quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads) and what your datasource allows, and make sure the second is not far smaller than the first, or the extra worker threads only queue for connections. Temporal workers have a maximum number of concurrent activity executions. That is a pool size by another name, and the same arithmetic applies: activities per second times average duration. Put issuer calls behind their own bulkhead, so a slow issuer costs you authorizations and nothing else.
mistake: Raising the thread count when the bottleneck is downstream. Authorizations slow down, someone doubles the pool from 64 to 128 threads, and latency gets worse: the database pool still has 20 connections, so 108 threads now queue for them, each holding a request in memory. It happens because thread count is the knob that's easy to turn. Look at the scarce resource first (Hikari's pending-connections metric, the issuer's error rate), size the pool to that limit, and put a bulkhead in front of the slow dependency.

compare.title: A bulkhead in Java and with coroutines

java.title: Bulkhead.java (solution, core of call)
java.html: public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { // a waiting caller blocks its platform thread here if (!permits.tryAcquire(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '" + name + "' is full"); } try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } }

kotlin.title: Bulkhead.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit class Bulkhead(private val name: String, maxConcurrent: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // fail fast, like Duration.ZERO in the Java version suspend fun <T> tryCall(work: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '$name' is full") try { return work() } finally { permits.release() } } // wait for a permit: the coroutine suspends and holds no thread while it waits suspend fun <T> call(work: suspend () -> T): T = permits.withPermit { work() } }

compare.note: Both protect the issuer the same way: at most N calls in flight. The difference is what waiting costs. The Java version blocks a platform thread in tryAcquire, so a thousand waiting callers are a thousand parked threads, which is why it needs a short maxWait. The coroutine Semaphore suspends, so a thousand waiting callers are a thousand small objects. kotlinx's Semaphore has no timed acquire; wrap the waiting call in withTimeout if you need a deadline.

worked.title: Size the authorization pool from measurements

steps.say: Measure first. Under a load test at the expected peak, the authorization path shows these numbers. Before reading on, estimate the pool size.
steps.code:
peak arrivals        400 / s
CPU per request      10 ms   (parse, validate, sign)
wait per request     140 ms  (issuer call)
cores                8
issuer contract      50 concurrent connections

steps.say: Little's law gives the concurrency the traffic needs: L = 400 x (0.010 + 0.140) = 400 x 0.15 = 60 requests in flight, so 60 threads if each request holds a thread for its whole life.

Check the CPU. 400 requests x 10 ms = 4 CPU-seconds every second, so 4 of the 8 cores are busy: 50 percent. Goetz's formula at that utilization agrees: 8 x 0.5 x (1 + 140/10) = 60. The box can carry the load.

Now the downstream. The issuer allows 50 concurrent connections, and each call holds one for 140 ms, so the issuer path tops out at 50 / 0.14 = 357 authorizations a second. That is below the 400 peak. A pool of 60 would leave 10 threads queued on the issuer's connections.

So the real answer is: put issuer calls behind a bulkhead of 50, size the pool near 60 so the non-issuer work keeps moving, and treat 357 a second as the service's real capacity. Getting to 400 is now a business question (a bigger contract with the issuer, or a second merchant client), not a pool setting.
steps.code: Bulkhead issuer = new Bulkhead("issuer", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)); ExecutorService auth = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60);

alt.html: val issuer = Bulkhead("issuer", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)) val auth = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60)

lab.title: Pool arithmetic and a bulkhead
steps: Run the tests. All nine fail.
Write the four PoolSizing methods. Each is one or two lines. Convert durations with d.toNanos() / 1e9 to get seconds as a double.
Write Bulkhead.call: tryAcquire with the max wait, throw BulkheadFullException if that fails, otherwise run the work and release the permit in a finally.
Run the tests until all nine pass.
hints: One test expects ioBound(3, 0.5, 10 ms, 30 ms) to be 2. In floating point, 3 x 0.5 x (1 + 10/30) comes out as 2.0000000000000004, and Math.ceil turns that into 3. Subtract a tiny amount (say 1e-9) before rounding up.
Semaphore.tryAcquire(long timeout, TimeUnit unit) with a zero timeout returns at once. It throws InterruptedException, which call may simply let through.
Don't wrap the work's exception. The test checks it gets the very same IOException back.

drill.title: Both laws from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Goetz's formula and Little's law. Then answer: (a) balance lookups arrive at 1,200 a second and take 40 ms; how many are in flight? (b) the lookup pool has 32 threads; what is its maximum throughput? (c) each lookup holds one of 20 database connections for 25 ms; what is the database path's limit?

answer.html:
threads = cores x utilization x (1 + W/C)
L = lambda x W

(a) L = 1,200 x 0.040 = 48 in flight
(b) lambda = L / W = 32 / 0.040 = 800 per second  (less than 1,200: the pool is too small)
(c) 20 / 0.025 = 800 per second  (the database caps you at the same rate)

So 48 threads would not help on their own: raise the connection limit too, or cut the 25 ms.

recap: CPU-bound pools want about one thread per core, from availableProcessors(), which respects container CPU limits.
Pools for work that waits use threads = cores x utilization x (1 + W/C), with W and C measured, not guessed.
Little's law, L = λ x W, gives the concurrency your traffic needs. Turned around, threads / latency is the most a pool can finish per second.
Every request also holds downstream resources. The smallest limit on the path (database pool, issuer connections, rate limit) is the real ceiling.
A bulkhead gives each dependency its own limit, so one slow dependency can't take every thread.

explain.prompt: Your manager asks why you can't just set every pool to 500 threads "to be safe". Explain, using the core count, Little's law and the database pool.
explain.answer: Threads only help while threads are the scarce thing. For CPU work the limit is the cores: beyond one thread per core, threads just take turns and add switching costs. For work that waits, Little's law tells us how many requests are in flight: arrival rate times latency. At 400 a second and 250 ms that is 100, so 500 threads would mostly sit idle, each with its own stack. And every request also needs things like a database connection. If the pool has 20 connections, threads beyond what 20 connections can serve just queue for them, holding memory and adding latency. So I size from the measured traffic, check CPU, cap it by the smallest downstream limit, and give slow dependencies their own bulkhead.

deeper.html:
Why aim for 80 percent CPU and not 100? Queueing theory has a short answer. In the simplest model of a single server with random arrivals (M/M/1), the average time in the system is W = S / (1 - ρ), where S is the service time and ρ is utilization. At 50 percent busy, a request spends 2 x S in the system. At 80 percent, 5 x S. At 90 percent, 10 x S. At 99 percent, 100 x S. Real systems are not M/M/1, but the shape holds: latency grows slowly at first and then very fast as you approach full use. Headroom is what keeps the 99th percentile sane during a burst.

Little's law has a subtle side that this lesson glossed over. The W in L = λ x W is the measured time in the system, including time spent queuing. If you add threads and requests now queue for a database connection instead of for a thread, W grows and throughput doesn't. That is exactly the debate on the loom-dev list before JEP 444 was finalized: more threads raise the ceiling only while threads are what requests wait for. Once the bottleneck moves downstream, the downstream sets λ.

The last tool is measurement. Time the queue wait and the run time of each task separately (lesson 9 of this track does this with beforeExecute and afterExecute). If queue wait dominates, the pool is too small for its traffic. If run time grew, look downstream.
